analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval of voting changes in states with records of voting-rights violations.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 219-212 on Aug. 24, 2021, with no Republican votes; the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have restored a key part of the Voting Rights Act that the Supreme Court struck down in 2013: the rule requiring states with recent records of voting discrimination to get approval from the Justice Department or a federal court before changing their election laws. It set a new, updated formula for deciding which states and localities are covered, based on their track record of voting-rights violations. It also made it easier for voters to challenge practices that dilute or deny minority votes, and required public notice of voting changes. The House passed it on a party-line vote, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Latino, Native, and language-minority voters in states and localities with recent records of voting-rights violations — would gain a federal check on election-rule changes, easier lawsuits against discriminatory practices, and public notice of changes to polling places and voting rules.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a new formula for deciding which states must get federal approval before changing election rules, triggered by a state or locality's record of voting-rights violations in the previous 25 years.
It makes it easier for voters to challenge practices that burden their vote, by spelling out factors courts must consider, including voter ID laws and changes to polling locations.
It requires states to publicly announce voting-rule changes within 48 hours and disclose polling-place resources and redistricting data, so voters can see what changed.
It adds 'retrogression' protection, barring changes that would make it harder for minority citizens to participate or elect their preferred candidates.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions would bear the cost of pre-clearing changes, providing documents to the Justice Department, and posting public notices. States and localities with records of violations would lose discretion over election administration for 10-year periods.
analysis.who_pays_short: State election officials in covered areas

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes federal preapproval and public-notice duties on state and local election officials, adding administrative cost and paperwork to running elections.

States and localities with past violations could see their election laws blocked or delayed for 10-year periods without a specific finding against each new change, which critics said treated jurisdictions as still untrustworthy long after the violations.
The bill drew zero Republican support in the House, and opponents argued the new preclearance formula intruded on state authority over elections under the Constitution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a workable, modernized preclearance formula courts had invalidated, plus stronger litigation tools for voters facing discriminatory changes — protections Congress created in 1965 and renewed repeatedly until 2013. The costs are real: jurisdictions with records of violations would face federal preapproval of election changes, and election officials would bear notice and paperwork burdens. The core trade-off is between state control over elections and federal protection of the right to vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in August 2021, the Senate received it in September, and it died there without a vote when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 4 on Aug. 24, 2021, by 219-212, with all 219 voting Democrats in favor and all 212 Republicans against.
The bill was received in the Senate on Sept. 14, 2021, and never received a vote in that chamber.
The bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on Jan. 3, 2023, without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials and parties that want maximum freedom to change election rules without federal review, since the new preclearance formula never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State officials freed from federal review

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 219 of 220 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to pass the bill.

against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against the bill on final passage.

against.role: House roll call on motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for a motion to send the bill back to committee, which failed 212-218.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote, and the chamber's filibuster rules meant it needed 60 votes to advance.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split exactly by party: all 219 voting Democrats for, all 212 Republicans against, and no Senate Republican ever considered it.

industries.industry: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions
industries.note: Jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations would have to get federal approval for election changes and post detailed public notices, giving up some control over election administration.

industries.industry: Officeholders and parties who benefit from drawing district maps
industries.note: By making it easier to win vote-dilution claims and covering redistricting changes, the bill raised the legal cost of district maps that weaken minority voting strength.
